blurb: Getting more AI for less: models that only wake the parts they need, cheaper attention, new designs and surprisingly capable small models.

cards.title: Only wake the experts you need

steps.p: In a standard ("dense") model, every parameter does work for every token. Bigger means slower and costlier for every word.
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model replaces one block in each layer with many smaller "expert" blocks.
steps.analogy: A hospital: you don't see every doctor, just the one or two your case needs.

steps.p: For each token, a small router network picks a couple of experts. Only those run; the rest stay idle.
So a model can have huge total knowledge but use only a small fraction per token. DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters but uses about 37 billion per token.
All the experts still have to sit in memory, ready to be picked. MoE saves computing, not storage.

cards.q: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B parameters but uses about 37B per token. Roughly what fraction is active?
cards.why: About 5.5%. It does the computing of a ~37B model per token while holding the knowledge of a 671B one.

cards.statement: In MoE language models, each expert usually specialises in a recognisable subject like biology or law.
cards.why: False. Despite the name, experts tend to specialise in messy, low-level patterns — punctuation, certain word types — not neat human subjects.

cards.q: Mixtral 8×7B has about 47B parameters, not 56B, because…
options: Attention and other parts are shared — only some blocks are copied into experts
cards.why: Only part is duplicated. The experts replace the feed-forward blocks; attention and embeddings are shared, so the total is less than 8 × 7B.

cards.title: Google's Switch Transformer (2021) sent each token to just one expert and grew to 1.6 trillion parameters.
cards.detail: Earlier designs used two or more experts per token. Switch showed one was enough, simplifying routing and cutting communication.

cards.statement: An MoE model needs less GPU memory than a dense model with the same number of active parameters.
cards.why: False. It needs much more: every expert must be stored. It's cheaper to compute, not cheaper to hold.

steps.p: For every token in a conversation, the model keeps notes (the KV cache). Long chats and many users mean huge memory use.
Grouped-query attention lets several attention "heads" share one set of notes, shrinking the cache several-fold.
steps.analogy: Instead of every student keeping their own full notes, each study group shares one set.

steps.p: Sliding-window attention lets each token look only at recent tokens. Information still travels further by hopping through layers.
DeepSeek's latent attention stores a compressed summary instead of full notes, cutting the cache by over 90%.
Standard attention compares every token with every other one, so doubling length quadruples the work. Research on "linear attention" tries to make it grow only in step with length.

visual.caption: Double the length, four times the comparisons.

options: The size of the KV cache, by sharing notes between heads
The number of words in the answer
cards.why: The KV cache. Fewer sets of stored notes means more memory for longer chats or more users.

cards.statement: With sliding-window attention, information can still travel further than the window by passing through several layers.
cards.why: True. Each layer passes information one window further, like a message relayed along a line of people.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V2's compressed attention cut its KV cache by about 93% compared with its previous model.
cards.detail: Storing a compressed summary instead of full notes let it serve far longer contexts and more users on the same hardware.

options: Make attention's cost grow in step with length, not with length squared
Read text in a straight line
cards.why: Grow with n, not n². Then doubling the text only doubles the work, making very long inputs practical.

cards.q: Which problem does grouped-query attention NOT solve?
options: The squared cost of comparing every token with every other in long prompts
cards.why: The comparisons remain. Sharing notes saves memory, but every token still has to be compared with every other.

cards.title: A different design: reading with a fixed-size memory

steps.p: A transformer keeps notes on every earlier token. Memory and work grow as the text gets longer.
State space models (like Mamba) read text in order, keeping only a fixed-size summary that's updated with each word.
steps.analogy: A transformer keeps every page on the desk; Mamba keeps a running notebook of fixed size.

steps.p: Mamba's twist: it decides, word by word, what's worth adding to its summary and what to forget.
Each new word costs the same time and memory no matter how long the text — great for very long inputs.
Exact recall of long strings is hard with a fixed-size summary, so hybrids mix a few attention layers with many Mamba layers.

cards.q: The key advantage of Mamba-style models when generating is…
options: Same memory and time per word, however long the text
cards.why: Constant cost. A fixed-size summary means the 100,000th word is as cheap as the 10th.

cards.statement: Pure state space models match transformers at copying long exact strings from earlier in the text.
cards.why: False. Squeezing everything into a fixed summary loses exact details, like a long phone number mentioned pages ago.

cards.q: Why do hybrid models mix attention layers with Mamba layers?
options: Attention gives precise recall; Mamba layers give efficiency
cards.why: Each covers the other's weakness. A few attention layers handle exact look-ups; the rest stay cheap.

cards.title: Mamba was created by Albert Gu and Tri Dao — and Tri Dao also invented FlashAttention.
cards.detail: So the same researcher helped make transformers much faster and built one of their best-known challengers.

cards.statement: RWKV is a design that reads text in order like an old RNN but can be trained in parallel like a transformer.
cards.why: True. It aims for a transformer's fast training with an RNN's cheap, steady generation.

steps.p: Small models run on phones and laptops: private, offline, instant and nearly free to use.
Distillation trains a small student to copy a big teacher's answers — including how confident the teacher is in each option.
steps.analogy: A student learning not just the right answer but the teacher's reasoning about why other answers are wrong.

visual.caption: The teacher's full guesses carry more information than just "cat".

steps.p: Pruning removes connections that barely matter. Quantization stores numbers with fewer bits. Both shrink models with modest quality loss.
Training on carefully chosen, high-quality data lets small models punch far above their size.
Phones now run small models directly — Apple's on-device model announced in 2024 has about 3 billion parameters.

cards.q: Apple's on-device model announced in 2024 has about how many parameters?
cards.why: About 3 billion. Small enough, with quantization, to run on an iPhone's own chip.

cards.statement: Pruning can remove a large share of a network's connections with only a small loss in quality.
cards.why: True. Many connections contribute very little. Removing them carefully keeps most of the ability.

cards.q: In distillation, why does the student learn from the teacher's full set of probabilities?
options: They show how the teacher ranks wrong answers too, which carries extra information
cards.hint: Look at the bar chart in step 2.
cards.why: Richer lessons. "Kitten 25%, car 0.1%" tells the student that a kitten is much closer to a cat than a car is.

cards.title: The 2015 paper that named "knowledge distillation" was co-written by Geoffrey Hinton and Jeff Dean.
cards.detail: With Oriol Vinyals, they showed a small model trained on a big model's softened guesses could capture much of its ability.

cards.title: Run a small model on your own laptop
cards.body: Free tools like Ollama run small open models entirely on your computer — no internet or account needed.
cards.challenge: Install Ollama and try a small model. Notice what it does well and where it struggles compared with a big chatbot.
